A significant aspect of quantum computing technology is the need for extremely cold temperatures, specifically one millikelvin. To facilitate research and testing, Fermilab has constructed an advanced cryogenic system called the Spinning Top Cryogenic System (STCS). Leveraging a previously developed "Aperios" refrigerator, the STCS incorporates enhancements to provide a large-scale, highly reliable cryogenic solution. With capabilities to cool an entire room to approximately 75 millikelvin, the system can support up to 100 simultaneous quantum processors, offering an innovative environment for quantum computing research. To address the need for efficient control and monitoring, Fermilab has developed a comprehensive software platform, referred to as The Aperture, designed to streamline operations within the cryogenic system, ensuring efficiency and reliability in experimental settings.

In this research, we examine various cryptographic implementations commonly found in popular Python libraries, identifying prevalent attacks that can compromise these vulnerabilities. These susceptible libraries encompass widely-used tools such as JWT, AES, MD5, and base64 encoding/decoding, which are prone to abuse due to their integration in over 100 influential Python applications. These attacks can be leveraged to execute malicious actions like forging tokens, extracting sensitive tokens, and extracting flags. These findings were presented at PyCon US 2021 and have been published as a whitepaper detailing our research.

Tagged images serve as the foundation for building knowledge in computer vision. Current approaches to automatically tag images either rely on weak labels, which are prone to errors, or manually tag a substantial number of images by domain experts, which is a time-consuming and costly process. To overcome these challenges, ensemble methods have been developed to leverage the collective opinion of multiple classifiers. Building on this concept, this paper presents a novel approach, the Voting-based Automatic Labeling Ensemble (VALUE), to efficiently scale up automatic image tagging in complex environments. VALUE consists of multiple taggers that use diverse sources to generate labels, and through a democratic process, selects the most reliable labels. When applied to street scenes, VALUE outperforms existing methods by a significant margin and achieves remarkable labeling accuracy close to 90%. The evaluation demonstrates that VALUE surpasses state-of-the-art methods by over 4% and close to 6% accuracy respectively, while also reducing the number of labeled samples needed by up to 80%.

Seismic reflectivity inversion plays a crucial role in oil and gas exploration by reconstructing underground geological structures. However, capturing non-uniform geology remains a significant challenge. In image processing, the sparsity of Laplacian priors has been utilized to represent non-uniform structures, and we propose a new penalty term, a Proximal Average (SPAN) penalty, to promote sparsity across varied regions. The SPAN penalty is applied directly to the penalty term without transformation, and we develop a proximal algorithm to solve the resulting optimization problem, combining p-Laplacian and the SPAN penalty. We extend this method to 2D reflectivity inversion and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments.

This study investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-like spaces, specifically focusing on BMOA, VMOA, and the space QC. We establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for composition operator semigroups to fall into the spaces BMOA or VMOA. Additionally, utilizing the L\"urothe-Schur algorithm, we determine the norm of the sum of n operators within the linear combination of composition operators, specifically CN(f, h), that fall into the space BMOA or VMOA.

We suggest two reliable methods to determine the scaling dimensions and other coefficients of spin model operators, emphasizing one novel approach based on universal scaling predictions for operator correlations between the two lowest ground states of finite-sized systems with open boundary conditions. This semi-infinite approach is particularly beneficial for models where computing ground state wavefunctions is difficult due to strong entanglement. We further examine universal scaling dimensions for operator and block spin correlations and present numerical results for these predictions across various one-dimensional quantum models. This analysis reveals a previously undocumented universal scaling dimension that applies to all local operators within a broad class of one-dimensional gapped quantum states, characterized by specific patterns in ground state entanglement and entanglement entropy corrections. We further apply this approach to derive an exact formula for the long-distance entanglement of block spin correlations in one-dimensional gapped quantum states and use this to determine the scaling dimensions of all symmetric operators in one quantum Haagerup model, a topological quantum phase that occurs in two dimensions.

We present a novel tagging scheme called the Extended International Phonetic Alphabet (EIPA), which encompasses 21 parts of speech and 24 morphological categories. In this study, we aimed to process old German texts from the 18th century, which posed significant challenges due to their complex orthography. To achieve a more reliable tagging outcome, we developed sets of predicted categories instead of single categories, thereby minimizing the probability of erroneous, albeit partially correct, tagging. Our tagging system, which combines a neural network-based model (PNN) and a unigram model, attained 69.1% exact prediction accuracy and 90.2% fuzzy prediction accuracy on historical German data, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art taggers on modern German texts, which reached 64.3% exact and 87.9% fuzzy exactitudes.

This research proposes a new class of fractional integrals applicable to functions with a specific type of non-continuous behavior, and it also examines the integrability principles for space-type fractional integrals in this context. Furthermore, it also considers the Minkowski inequality and a new type of Hardy inequality in this framework.

This study introduces an extended state machine method derived from UML, adapted for precise city governance requirements specifications. Building upon this method, a pioneering smart assistant has been developed, capable of automatically converting user-inputted cities' requirements into formal extended state machine representations. The smart assistant streamlines formal specification, reducing cognitive load and enhancing user experience. Furthermore, the authors emphasize the significance of preliminary research to uncover the underlying causes of state machine complexity, a crucial step towards mitigating state explosion.

This paper introduces an advanced quantum error correction approach for surface codes, building upon the influential hidden-inverses protocol developed by Terhal in 2018. The proposed method involves a strategic addition of ancilla qubits, which possess intrinsic inherent recovery properties, enabling direct intervention in logical qubit computation without necessitating additional resources. For instance, when a logical qubit is subjected to an Xn or Zn error, the proposed protocol inverts the error order to shift the error to the rightmost position for measurement. This measurement outcome then facilitates error recovery. In the rightward direction of computation, repeated applications of the protocol are feasible, ultimately error-free. Furthermore, this scheme offers a significant advantage by eliminating ancilla errors in error recovery and reducing the number of required ancillas to log N, where N represents the number of error-corrected logical qubits.

Equivalence relations can be viewed as a form of'symmetry' within categories, with weak representations being fully faithful. By extending this concept to categories with regular structure, we find that full representations require more substantial conditions, such as being epimorphisms in elementary categories. In categories with regular structure, however, it is sufficient for preorders to be represented as weakly cocartesian, and in elementary categories, this property becomes a criterion for being cocartesian. Furthermore, we identify two key conditions under which weak preorder representations become full: being regular in elementary categories and satisfying a pullback condition with absolute retracts in regular categories. Similarly, we establish criteria for equivalence relation representation: being finitarily injective with a retracted domain allows for weak representations to become full in elementary categories, with a single condition applying to regular categories.

Using a bivariate extreme value model, we analyzed simultaneous extreme weather events in two Australian coastal towns, Exmouth and Port Lincoln, focusing on significant wave heights and wave periods. Our examination incorporated four types of thresholds and four prediction time frames to examine the interconnections between these extreme events. Experiments using simulated data and real wave data from Exmouth and Port Lincoln helped us validate and understand the relationships between simultaneous extreme weather events in these regions.

Multimodal models that combine text and images are crucial in computer vision, and VT-CLIP, a new variant of the CLIP model, is proposed to leverage text information more effectively by leveraging image-based features to improve text descriptions. The approach leverages the strengths of pre-trained language models to encode text information more accurately, and our experiments on a variety of tasks, including few-shot and zero-shot benchmarks, reveal that VT-CLIP outperforms CLIP in multiple recognition and retrieval tasks, with consistent results across different datasets and tasks.

This study introduces universal strategies for managing noise in matrix systems, effectively applying to a wide range of systems including Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems as well as orthogonal ensembles of operators. Our fast switching techniques for neutralizing noise within operator ensembles are shown to be equivalent in efficacy to those employed for directly quenching noisy states. By characterizing the envelope of noise within ensembles of unitary operators subject to Gaussian noise, we establish a relationship between our technique and continuous monitoring methods that combat Hermitian operator noise. Notably, our approach is applicable even to systems with time-varying operators.

We identify the first non-trivial homotopy groups in a specific type of spectrum called the quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum, specifically $\infty$-truncated versions, and then use this insight to find the cohomology with specific constraints in certain spaces linked to a particular group, and further this to understand the cohomology with specific constraints in a related spectrum and compare it to a theory introduced by another researcher.

Given a quasi-excellence local pair (R, m) of characteristic p and an m-primary ideal I in R, we define the tight Hilbert function f_{I,n} as the vector space dimension of R[I^n] over R, and f_{I,n} as its corresponding values. The function f_{I,n} exhibits limiting behavior, specifically the tight Hilbert function, the tight Hilbert series, the tight Frobenius-pseudo-Frobenius number, and the tight Frobenius-integral-valued function, which all converge to their respective constants or functions, denoted by \bar{f}_{I,n}, \bar{f}_{I,z}, \bar{f}_{IP,F,p}, and \bar{f}_{I,F,p}(z), respectively. The relationship f_{I,n} ≥ f_{I,n-1} holds, and these variables asymptotically approach their respective constants or functions, which is a key insight we provide in this paper. The result is further extended to equidimensional local pairs (R, m) of characteristic p and mixed dimension s by defining \bar{F}_{I,F,p}(z) as \bar{F}_{I,F,p}(z) - (d-1)z, which has a leading coefficient \frac{e(F,I)}!(p-1)^d z^d and all other coefficients dependent on I and R. The result is proven for F-singularity local

Model evaluation and comparison are highly important in the deployment of artificial intelligence, particularly in the field of medical imaging. However, various research groups often fail to match the potential due to issues stemming from lack of standardization of evaluation and comparison methods. Existing solutions, such as those in radiology (e.g., DICOM-R, highdicom-r), do not meet the same needs in pathology. We propose a solution, Highdicom, a Python library that facilitates standardized encoding of diagnostic tests, machine intelligence outputs in medical imaging, and related findings, for both radiology and pathology. This library aligns with prevailing best practices and industry standards in medical imaging, and adheres to high-quality software development principles, allowing both pathologists and radiologists to be treated equivalently. Highdicom supports the creation of universally accepted machine intelligence models, enabling seamless exchange of data and evaluation in both pathology and radiology.

The Bach tensor, which represents the variation of the Gibbons-Hawking-York boundary term in the Einstein-Hilaction, has been underexplored in literature. We derive the associated Noether currents and show they generate diffeomorphisms. Consequently, the currents can be integrated to yield charges, which are further broken down into magnetic and electric components. To be specific, the magnetic part aligns with a Viroro algebra, while the electric part relates to a zero mode of a Kac-Moody algebra. Notably, the magnetic component dominates in high-entropy conditions. A specific form of the magnetic charges enables a straightforward calculation of the holographic entropy current. Moreover, the magnetic charges exhibit a power-law scaling behavior in relation to the entropy current components, especially in the vicinity of black hole horizons. This behavior is equivalent to that of the Noether charges derived from the bulk diffeomorphism invariance.

In recent years, deep learning techniques have been successfully applied to analyze DNA sequences in various research areas, achieving accurate predictions of DNA function. However, this approach often relies on more advanced and more complex models, which work well on DNA sequences from similar species but struggle with sequences from distant species. In addition, the unsupervised learning of DNA features remains an area that has received relatively little research focus. In this study, we investigated and compared various deep learning models for extracting features from unknown DNA sequences in an unsupervised setting. Our findings indicate that unsupervisedly learned features from DNA sequences are comparable to those derived from traditional methods, such as one-hot encoding and the k-mer method. Moreover, our research reveals that combining multiple embedding techniques can significantly improve performance.

The impact of surface modification on the metal-insulator transition of a 5-unit-cell thick V$_2$O$_3$(0001) film was studied. Results showed significant variations in structural parameters within the film, influenced heavily by surface termination and growth conditions. Notably, changing the growth environment from vacuum to an oxygen atmosphere and subsequently switching between V and O termination led to distinct surface modifications. Using first-principles calculations, researchers found that a mixed spin configuration in the ($V$)$^+$-($V$)$^+$-termination yielded a metallic phase consistent with experiment, whereas an ($O$)$^+$-($V$)$^+$-termination with a localized electron in the last vanadium layer led to an insulating phase. These findings demonstrate that in extremely thin films, structural characteristics are dominated by surface modifications, which can be controlled via various methods.

The general form of Lie-Poisson brackets, derived from the theory of differential forms, reveals that a Lie-Poisson structure can be derived from a specific, universally applicable collection of functions in the sense of Frobenius, encompassing the Casimir functions of its dense orbit symplectic leaf. For a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, we identify a specific collection of functions $V$, invariant under the coadjoint action, along with parameters $r$ and $s$ that determine its dimension. These parameters correspond to the codimensions of two specific ideals within $\mathfrak{g}^*$. It is then shown that the universal Clebsch canonization of the Lie-Poisson structure on $\mathfrak{g}$, consisting of functions $(z, \zeta)$, with the same dimensions as $(V, \mathfrak{g})$, exists, along with a corresponding Poisson map $\Phi$ from $\mathfrak{g}$, where $z$ equals its coadjoint orbit value $\mathcal{O}_\mu$, and where $\Phi$ maps to the Clebsch canonization of its Lie-Poisson structure, restricted to the coadjoint orbit $\mathcal{O}_\mu$. Our recent analysis of 2,412 anomalies detected in KMTNet time-series data has led to the identification of a sample of secondary-field planets discovered through microlensing. A total of 1,099 anomalies were observed in the Gaia source catalog, and subsequently, a specialized team analyzed the source fields of these anomalies using the KMTNet data. Of these anomalies, 60 planetary events were discovered and confirmed as distinct from their corresponding primary events, with the planet-to-host mass ratio ranging from 2.2 x 10^-5 to 3.7 x 10^-2 and a median mass ratio of 2.1 x 10^-3. A comparative analysis of the detected anomalies and stellar anomalies revealed similarities in their light curve characteristics, suggesting that the observed differences may be due to the detection method rather than the anomalies' intrinsic properties. Our research indicates an estimated 1,182 additional planetary events in 2018, with 70% of these anomalies exhibiting non-conservative mass ratios and predominantly residing in the 10^3 - 10^5 M_Jupiter mass range.

A series of two technical reports aims to explore the potential of a mathematical framework developed by the authors in a previous work. This framework enables the manipulation of conservation laws that underpin partial differential equations. This part of the report focuses on the pressure and body force terms within the Navier-Stokes equations, examining how the theory can fully determine these terms through the presented framework. As an example, the paper discusses a simple model that effectively captures the complex micro to macro transitions in fluid flow. Furthermore, the work demonstrates the unique nature of expressing the pressure term within the energy equation in relation to the pressure reading used to express energy fluxes in the Navier-Stokes equations. This representation is typically fixed in engineering practices and thus overlooked in traditional mathematical treatments. Utilizing the method developed in this report, the pressure can be tailored to align with specific micro-macro transition scenarios. Utilizing the framework, the work generalizes previous mathematical results that focused on incompressible fluids, examining the potential for local existence and uniqueness of solutions under weak initial conditions. As an example, the work proves well-posedness for zero initial velocity and a specific form of initial energy that incorporates a positive definite Hessian for the density. Notably, this work reveals the possibility of introducing an arbitrary barotropic equation of state into the Navier-Stokes equations, which is particularly useful for modeling fluids with phase transitions.

A prominent issue in the banking sector is managing Non-Performing Loans, which poses
significant challenges due to their unpredictable nature. Identifying such loans and
classifying them into risk categories is a crucial step in mitigating this issue.
However, machine learning models' effectiveness in addressing the associated
non-linearity and unbalanced data challenges remains uncertain. This research aims to
address these issues by implementing various machine learning models and feature
importance techniques, including Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Support Vector
Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Principal Component Analysis, to predict binary
classes and reduce the dimensionality of the feature space, respectively. The study's
results reveal that Random Forest outperforms other models and that combining age and
income features yields optimal outcomes.

We introduce the concept of Dyck trails, which are path configurations defined by a grid structure. These path configurations exhibit intriguing connections to other areas of study. The link between them and chromatic symmetric functions reveals that the chromatic symmetric functions of certain graph classes are aligned with those of Dyck trail configurations. The Dyck trail configurations themselves exhibit non-zero chromatic symmetric functions that possess a structure reminiscent of elementary and complete homogeneous symmetric functions within a quadratic range. We also demonstrate that these symmetric functions adhere to a particular type of inequality known as log-concavity. Furthermore, we establish a parallel between the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck trails and a broader framework involving q-analogs of combinatorial concepts such as weak compositions, placements, and fixing indices. We conclude by presenting two additional areas of investigation related to these path configurations.

Convolutional neural networks, particularly in image recognition tasks, heavily rely on directional kernel operations that inherently preserve image structure. This research investigates the effects of applying various sampling strategies in coordinate space on grid-based images and introduces an innovative direction convolution operation. Notably, our proposed method is computationally more efficient and scalable on modern graphics processing units compared to adaptive sampling techniques. We also showcase the effectiveness of integrating our direction convolution operation with residual networks, achieving outstanding results in the MNIST, SVHN, and CelebA datasets.

We use the unitary dual of special orthogonal groups over finite fields to establish the curvature for linear periods defined by Chang and Gan-Gurevich, and then derive a novel relative trace formula that will help examine the curvature further.

We have carried out two-point correlation function calculations in lattice QCD to determine b, c, and charmless hadron masses, with an emphasis on two light meson masses to investigate the dependence of the calculated top quark mass on the masses of the pseudoscalar and scalar hadrons that serve as interpolators for the quark correlation functions. This investigation reveals a substantial variation in the calculated top quark mass, with an increase of approximately 150 MeV when substituting the correlation function based on bottom quark interpolators with those using charm quark interpolators, and an even more pronounced effect when replacing light meson masses based on charmless interpolators. This significant variation underscores the importance of carefully selecting the quark and hadron masses, highlighting the need for further theoretical and computational advancements.

We focus on $\chi$-boundedness issues related to subgraphs with maximum degree $\Delta$ in graphs that exhibit almost regular characteristics. Specifically, the case of $K_r$-free graphs is examined more closely, where the known results indicate the lower and upper bounds for $\beta$ in $\chi$-boundedness. For instance, when considering graphs with maximum degree $\Delta$, $\Delta$ is given by the formula $\frac{(r-2)N}{r-1}$, where $N$ represents a large number. A key result in our study demonstrates that graphs with maximum degree $\Delta$ are sequentially edge-$r$-tintable over the subset of vertices, denoted as $V(G)$, under specific conditions. Specifically, the condition for tintability is that the number of vertices with degree $\Delta$ is less than or equal to $2N$, which is a significant result in the context of our study. Furthermore, our study also introduces new upper bounds for the case of graphs that are not just $K_r$-free but also chromatic number bounded by $A$ for the purpose of $\chi$-boundedness. A notable finding for this case is that $\chi$-boundedness can be achieved using the formula $\Delta + 2A + 2r + 2$ for large enough values of $N$. In addition, our study also introduces another upper bound for a more relaxed case, which is given by
We establish a hypercontractive inequality in the context of a weighted Berman space involving $n$ variables defined on a finite measure space with distinct weights.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused a significant global crisis, with COVID-19 pneumonia being a major cause of mortality. Due to the risks associated with X-ray and CT examinations, which involve exposure to ionizing radiation, patients with COVID-19 pneumonia are often reluctant to undergo conventional imaging. This paper proposes a COVID-19 pneumonia detection system utilizing low-dose CT examinations, which employs a time-distributed capsule network for feature extraction and a binary classifier for classification, combining the expressiveness of TCN and TCN with TCN architecture. This approach has achieved outstanding results, demonstrating performance on par with human-level expertise, with an accuracy of 90.6%, precision of 90.0%, recall of 90.4%, and F1-score of 0.90. Furthermore, this method's effectiveness has been validated through ablation studies, which have confirmed its performance on three public datasets.

This chapter provides a detailed examination of utilizing low-Earth orbit. It covers
essential concepts of orbital mechanics and methods for maneuvering spacecraft,
and discusses strategies to maintain a safe and efficient use of the shared space in low-Earth orbit.

We introduce a novel method for automatically creating high-order coarse quadrilateral meshes on CAD models by leveraging integer linear programming. Our integer linear formulation can be solved to produce optimal coarse meshes, and it can also be used to refine pre-existing lower-order meshes into higher-order coarse meshes. The proof of optimality for this formulation is grounded in the convexity of the variable domains involved. Our approach incorporates edge-coincidence constraints and novel concepts such as odd-holes and even-holes. To facilitate faster solution times, we incorporate pre-processing techniques including collapsible columns and lower-bounding height values. Our coarse mesh generator is publicly available online.

The sample correlation coefficient offers a practical method for examining relationships between variables. We have developed an analytical formula for its moment of order $q$ under permutations of the sample. Our results demonstrate that the expected value of the sample correlation's $q$th moment yields significant statistical insights. We have used this to derive an analytical expression for estimating the population correlation's distribution. We have used Monte Carlo simulations to compare the efficacy of our estimator with that of the maximum-likelihood method.

We propose an approach to solving Hamiltonian constraints in general relativity by employing a S-matrix framework with spatial wave packet states. Focusing on two distinct approaches involving either two or three spherical atoms, we analyze the radial momentum distribution of a specific source. Additionally, we examine how this approach can be adapted to other theories such as non-relativistic quantum mechanics and massless scalar fields in anti-de Sitter space.

This paper presents a universal stabilization strategy for solutions of the 3D and 4D Navier-Stokes equations in both periodic and unbounded domains. The control inputs are designed as interior, localized, and proportional norms of the state variables to achieve stability in critical Sobolev and Besov spaces, which is an improvement over previous control strategies that required the use of open loops and were applied to smaller $L^q$ spaces. The control approach is implemented using a finite dimensional state feedback control law to make it practically feasible. The proof for stability is built on three key tools: the compactness of the control's influence on the system, the separation of trajectories, and the Schauder fixed point theorem. The methodology used here also applies to the 2D Navier-Stokes equations in any spatial dimension and to the 1D through 3D Navier-Stokes equations in its critical $L^2$-based Sobolev space by its proof remains valid even after replacing the compactness assumption with the help of a unique global attractor and a finite embedding theorem.

LitMind is a lexicographical database that enables users to create digital minds based on established psychological theories. As such, it serves as a dynamic and open dictionary that can be updated by anyone, incorporating a diverse range of concepts from various domains. Unlike traditional dictionaries, LitMind focuses on describing the context and emotional nuances behind each term, providing a more holistic understanding of their meanings. The platform is specifically designed to be user-friendly, making it easy to share, edit, and expand the database through simple copy-paste actions. With its flexible structure and extensive range of concepts, LitMind empowers everyone to share their knowledge and wisdom, allowing for the creation of mental frameworks and knowledge networks.

The LIME method, originally developed for machine learning models, has recently been adapted for recommendation systems to enhance transparency and trustworthiness in user interactions and system maintenance. However, LIME-RS, the specific application of LIME to recommendation systems, has not thoroughly been evaluated in a previous research study. By adapting the analysis framework proposed by Becigneul et al. (2019) to LIME-RS, we identified four primary shortcomings in its explanation generation capabilities, namely, understanding its limits, explaining surprising items, indicating a model's confidence, and ensuring its reliability across various contexts. Through experiments conducted on three datasets and additional analyses, we discovered the underlying reasons for these limitations, ultimately providing potential solutions for improving the effectiveness of LIME-RS in the future.

Researchers have developed and experimentally tested the design and performance characteristics of a new type of phase-sensitive amplifier based on mid-infrared interacting quantum networks. The proposed design utilizes near-surface InAs/AlAs quantum wells to achieve this, with an innovative method to control Fermi level pinning. By applying a thin layer of highly doped semiconductors, the impact of surface pinning on the carrier distribution within the quantum structure can be minimized. This allows for greater control over the quantum system's behavior and can significantly enhance its performance as a narrowband coherent amplifier. Experimental results show the use of quantum interference to synchronize the pump and signal frequencies within a specific quantum transition, with corresponding increases in the amplifier's gain and efficiency.

In this paper, we investigate the robust generalization capabilities of models incorporating local data validation. Our analysis reveals under what conditions local learning can lead to better robust generalization than non-local models. To examine this issue in controlled settings, we developed a simple linear model with a localized verification mechanism and found that its robust generalization ability is superior in settings with distinct linear subgroups. Our results also show a relationship between the size of these subgroups and the size of the local data needed for improved robust generalization. An extensive analysis was also performed on K-means clustering in both noise-free and noisy environments, and we found that the local data size required for K-means to outperform more advanced LIP methods is substantial for certain dimensions.

Our previous research significantly reduced the time complexity of the Sinkhorn algorithm, linearly scaling the time to update the kernel for the first time. Building on this work, we now address a key issue of approximating the optimal coupling by achieving a precise calculation in the same time complexity. We've developed a new fast, linear-scale iterative method that works by maintaining a triangular matrix structure with collinear edges for efficient storage and updating. This approach leverages its storage and update efficiencies to solve a convex optimization problem by adapting a variant of Newton's algorithm. We've successfully applied this technique to real-world datasets, achieving impressive improvements in the performance of tasks such as image denoising, super-resolution, and single-cell clustering, with up to a 50% reduction in the time required to converge compared to previous work.

The young star AU Mic has been the subject of two distinct theories regarding its activity level. One study suggested that it is the most magnetically active and FUV luminous main sequence star, indicating "crown" activity. In contrast, a more recent study found no signs of FUV emission from the star, suggesting quiescent "coronal" activity. The conflicting findings prompted a deeper investigation. Our research focused on the variability of the far ultraviolet light emitted by AU Mic, specifically looking at its effects on the circumstellar disk, variability in the system, and AU Mic's effect on the planets AU Mic b and c. Observations of the star revealed no signs of FUV variability, contradicting expectations based on past studies and the expected planets' effects. Our findings also indicate that FUV flares are unlikely to cause significant water photodissociation, which is contrary to earlier predictions. Our research also suggests that FUV emission from AU Mic is unlikely to contribute to the observed strength of the water molecules in the circumstellar disk.

Moving charges through a non-conductive medium with high density and in the presence of electromagnetic radiation, experience what's known as the Kozyrev drag force. The drag force depends on the angle of movement and is determined by a combination of the medium's properties and radiation intensity. The drag force arises from a cross-correlation between moving charges and time-varying charge distributions in the medium, resulting in continuous radiation emission and loss of kinetic energy. The radiation patterns produced by a moving charge differ significantly from those produced in a non-conductive medium, with differences depending on the angle of movement and medium properties. Our analysis is based on non-relativistic speeds and non-conductive medium densities.

In the realm of machine learning, handling class imbalance is a critical issue, particularly when training classifiers. The assumption that data samples are independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) is often violated in cases of significant class imbalance, where rare classes are poorly represented. This paper proposes a novel approach to tackle the class imbalance problem by leveraging the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) classifier, which does not rely on the i.i.d. assumption. The proposed method involves assigning a probability to each sample based on the proportion of labels among the $k$ nearest neighbors, effectively re-weighting the training data to mitigate class imbalance. Experiments were conducted using the UCI dataset, and the k-NN algorithm showed superiority over oversampling techniques in addressing the class imbalance problem.

We have identified 13 new, highly luminous quasars, discovered by the SkyMapper Southern Survey, with rest-frame $z$-band luminosities exceeding $10^{46}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and located at redshifts 3.05 to 4.38. These quasars, along with 22 similar objects, comprise a sample of 25 of the most luminous quasars at redshifts greater than 3, with corresponding spectral energy distributions derived from their photometry. By combining our 37 quasars, along with 104 other known quasars at redshifts 3 to 4.38, we estimated the luminosity function at rest-frame $M_{1450}$ to be $A=0.77^{+0.11}_{-0.13}$ and $\gamma=3.29^{+0.12}_{-0.12}$. Notably, our results indicate a decrease in the space density of extremely luminous quasars, with rest-frame $M_{1450} > -27.5$, from $z=3$ to $z=4$, at greater than 4$\sigma$ confidence, with the space density decreasing by a factor of 10 or more, and a transition occurring at $z\sim3.5$. We have investigated the charge-tunneling spectrum of a quantum dot and a high-energy gap superconducting island using sensing techniques. Differentiating between two charge transfer mechanisms - the Keldysh mechanism and the Andreev mechanism - has been achieved. It was observed that the Andreev mechanism dominates when the quantum dot is close in energy to the superconducting island's gap. Moreover, the dependence of the energy gap on the electrostatic potential of the island exhibits nonlinearity when represented on a full counting statistics diagram, indicating the presence of multi-charge excitations. These findings provide significant insight into the design of hybrid quantum devices.

We analyze solutions to a system of $N$ conservation laws that have an entropic slope, a property influenced by a Kruzkov-type entropy-entropy flux pair. This property restricts solutions to the system and, under specific conditions, ensures uniqueness of solutions in certain scenarios. These conditions typically involve either a strictly monotonic entropic slope or the inclusion of additional criteria like being a shock wave solution. In this work, we explore the potential for weakening some of the strict assumptions currently used in the literature and demonstrate the utility of generalized contractions applicable to a broader class of systems, including those that are not total variational.

Creating digital dreams has long been the goal of computer vision, specifically in always generating dynamic camera views from a single image. The application of generative adversarial networks, particularly conditional generative adversarial models, has led to significant advancements in this area, surpassing traditional multi-view geometry methods. However, the results from conditional adversarial models have been inconsistent, particularly when dealing with complex scenes. In response, we propose DiffDreamer, the latest in diffusion models for single-view perpetual view generation. The model effectively integrates image editing and view synthesis tasks through its training process, leveraging unconditioned training to expand its applicability. The results show that DiffDreamer surpasses traditional GAN-based approaches and demonstrates robust synthesis capabilities across diverse and intricate scenes.

Industrial processes are frequently organized into multiple units to enhance efficiency and control, resulting in interconnected networks where each unit relies on shared input resources. The interdependence between units necessitates the consideration of dynamic variations in shared resources when designing industrial processes. The impact of industrial fluctuations on control, performance, and decision-making processes has been extensively studied, yet there is a notable lack of research on the influence of these dynamics on the management of individual units. This paper addresses the challenge of managing individual units within a networked process under dynamic variations in shared resources. Using a stochastic modelS for network process dynamics, this study demonstrates the development of predictive, optimal decision-making, and control strategies for individual units. The methods proposed rely solely on empirical data, without requiring assumptions or simplifications. The results show that these data-driven strategies perform significantly better than traditional approaches in terms of various performance metrics.

We investigate the dynamics of a thin liquid layer on a vertical fibre as it undergoes the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The instability is enhanced by assuming that the liquid moves without resistance at the centre of the fibre, which contrasts with previous models that assumed uniform viscosity throughout. This assumption has a significant impact on the growth rate of long-wave perturbations and results in a behaviour that is intermediate between the cases with and without slip at the fibre surface. We further explore the shallower deposition profiles resulting from this scenario and examine how they differ from the profiles predicted by the no-slip model. Lastly, we propose a method for determining the size of the fibre based on the characteristics of the resulting deposition profiles.

We investigate the Lipschitz stability of the Hunter-Saxton model, a geometric model of an oriented rope that features finite-speed wave propagation and shock formation. We establish that a key tool, backtracking, allows for the quantification of the distance between two Hunter-Saxton fields. Furthermore, we explore the problem of characterizing geodesics within the Hunter-Saxton metric space and investigate how the absence of the 1-metric approach leads to a breakdown in the smoothness of the geodesic extension problem.

Evaluating scoliosis using ultrasound is an effective approach, particularly when comparing the reliability of the imaging process against traditional methods. A study was conducted to examine whether robotic ultrasound and manual scoliosis assessment yield the same results, and if so, if there are any significant differences in the process. In the study, robotic ultrasound was administered to 20 scoliosis patients, and data from this process was compared with that from a standard manual ultrasound examination. By analyzing joint data, researchers observed that robotic imaging produced the same curvature as manual imaging but with reduced variability. This reduction in variability was attributed to the consistent spinal angle measurement, and as a result, it was concluded that robotic scoliosis imaging has a high level of reliability.

This paper introduces an method for creating synthetic speech of variable durations based on the median duration of its counterpart. Traditional speech synthesis systems, like those utilizing Hidden Markov Models, often neglect the median duration characteristic, and a more effective approach is proposed. This novel method involves training a model to predict the ratio of actual to median speech duration, thereby enhancing the accuracy of synthesized speech. To validate this approach, a dataset of 1,061 duration pairs from three distinct languages (Arabic, Spanish, and English) was used. To circumvent the challenge of limited ground truth data, the study employs a variable-length sequence-to-sequence model, specifically designed for regression. Notably, the method's characteristics, particularly the pre-trained model's state transition matrix, are revealed, offering a novel application in speech synthesis.

The rise of the internet has facilitated communication, enabling individuals to share their views freely. However, this freedom often goes unregulated by traditional institutions. Users have access to various online forums, such as blogs and social media platforms. Unfortunately, this openness to diverse opinions has led to the prevalence of offensive content. Consequently, researchers have been working to develop automated systems to detect and prevent hate speech on these platforms. Our study focuses on identifying hate speech on Facebook by incorporating the use of hashtags and culminating in the development of a novel, feature-based classification model. This model exhibits superior performance compared to existing approaches.

In Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) architectures, which aim to optimize resource allocation across various tasks by sharing intermediate features, determining the optimal number of shared layers is challenging. This problem is particularly complex due to the significant impact of network width and interconnects on performance. This study investigates the concept of shared features in MIMO networks in detail, focusing on the non-intuitive results of their utilization. Experimental results show that reducing the number of shared layers can be beneficial in certain scenarios. Notably, our findings indicate that too many layers hinder the distinctiveness of their representations. Moreover, we observe that the effectiveness of feature sharing is significantly affected by the width of the networks, with many MIMO configurations failing to reach parity with their fully connected counterparts. Finally, we reveal that not all networks within a shared layer contribute equally, suggesting that only certain parameters should be trained.

Historical manuscripts hold immense cultural significance due to the wealth of information they contain about history, language, and other disciplines. These documents, however, present a significant challenge due to their aged and fragmented condition. Despite growing interest, the scarcity of complete handwritten manuscript datasets continues to impede research. This study provides a comprehensive compilation of datasets previously employed in historical manuscript analysis, along with descriptions of their content and sources. We also examine the primary tasks performed using these datasets, and highlight areas for improvement, ultimately aiming to accelerate the advancement of the field.

To improve position accuracy in industrial robots, we propose a novel approach that utilizes light and sound feedback from unseen surfaces utilizing time-of-flight and time-of-arrival measurements. Complementary to this, we develop a method to efficiently utilize this extra feedback through the model-based flatness-based control framework. To ensure optimal performance, we create an auxiliary algorithm for fine-tuning the sensor. Our design's robustness against external disturbances and variable sensor parameters robustness is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and experimental results.

In studies of recurrent events like heart attacks and other chronic conditions, traditional statistical methods are often limited. They focus solely on event frequency, ignoring the complex interplay between experiences over time and individual life paths. To address this gap, we propose a new framework for understanding and analyzing recurring events like myocardial infarctions. We categorize these events into distinct types based on their underlying causes, using insights from existing literature to create an event taxonomy that can be applied to a broader range of experiences over time. To capture the dynamic nature of these events and their relationship with time-varying factors, we employ recurrent neural networks. When sufficient data is available, we can use representation learning to automatically create a meaningful event classification system. However, when such data is scarce, we turn to supervised learning methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through analyses of patients with myocardial infarctions, showing its potential to shed new light on experience classifications, patient subgrouping, and the effects of interventions.

An electrostatic program, called Molecular Continuum, has been developed for modeling biological molecules interacting with metal surfaces, an application underexplored in computational chemistry. This program addresses multiple metal surfaces and handles molecules larger than 1000 atoms at 1 femtosecond time steps. An issue with the method is that it requires individual surface calculations when a molecule approaches different surface areas during simulations. A new, efficient integration scheme, called MC-IC, has been proposed to pre-calculate surface calculations and store them for immediate use in simulations, reducing computational costs and increasing efficiency by up to 90% when using flat surfaces, or 30% when using more complex compound surfaces.

The vertices in a graph, denoted by G and labeled with V, have the ability to distinguish between other vertices, also referred to as discriminators. A subset of vertices, labeled S, can identify every pair of vertices as long as their distances differ. The smallest possible value of S that satisfies this condition is defined as the dimension of G. Determining whether a graph G has a dimension less than or equal to K can be solved in time O(2^k * n + m), where the variables G and V represent the number of vertices and edges, respectively. In this work, we present two algorithms that efficiently solve the metric dimension problem by parameterizing it with respect to two other parameters: the number of feedback vertex subsets and the number of vertex covers. The first of these parameters is solved in time O((s * 2^s * k + n + m)), while the second parameter has a parameterized complexity with time complexity O((2^k + n + m)). Additionally, we present two other parameterizations with respect to variables: induced subgraph duality number and graph boolean width. The first of these parameters has a parameterized complexity with time complexity O((k^k * n + m)), while the second parameter has a parameterized complexity with time complexity O((2^k * n + m)).

Inspired by directed geometry, this study investigates power structures defined on directed spaces and their inherent characteristics, establishing key properties such as associativity, commutativity, and more. Notably, specific power frameworks associated with directed intervals possess additional identities and DF-units, and it's shown that the framework for the directed interval has two DF-units in particular. Additionally, this research demonstrates the framework's applicability to various mathematical spaces, including $\mathbb{R}^n$, simplicial sets, CW complexes, and directed graphs, and explores its relevance to directed categories and preorders.

This study focuses on the relationship between atmospheric water vapor and precipitation in the Earth's atmosphere. Since the amount of water vapor is heavily influenced by temperature, this feedback mechanism is expected to have a notable impact on the formation of precipitation. Utilizing the Community Earth System Model, we conducted simulations of a hypothetical "hot greenhouse" Earth scenario with an average surface temperature of 350 K. By adjusting key precipitation processes, we were able to maintain average surface temperatures consistent with past hot greenhouse Earth scenarios from the Neoproterozoic era. Our results indicate that the increased water vapor present in warmer climates leads to an increase in precipitation intensity but a decreased frequency of precipitation events. Notably, precipitation patterns in our simulations show a strong correlation with local temperature, leading to the formation of intense, localized precipitation events. This research suggests that warmer climates may be more prone to the formation of intense, localized precipitation events.

We've established a twistor construction of higher-spin extensions to Yang-Mills theory, and this framework reveals a two-fold connection. First, it confirms the equivalence of two "dual" self-dual Yang-Mills theories, and second, it suggests a new, simple equation that may serve as a higher-spin version of self-dual Yang-Mills theory, characterized by a specific geometric property of a twistor function's world scalar wavefunction, leading to the free field equation when that property is absent.

Deep neural networks have become a standard choice for solving medical image analysis tasks, driven by their impressive performance. However, their practical application is often hindered by the presence of label noise due to limitations in medical imaging technology and the availability of such images. Prior approaches to mitigating this issue typically rely on assumptions about noise distribution, limiting their practicality. Our solution, called BS-LRM, tackles this challenge by employing Bayesian statistics to derive bounds on class probabilities, thereby providing label noise-free estimates. This method needs no assumptions about noise distribution, no additional training, and can be seamlessly integrated with existing data classification models. Our approach was tested on a public dataset consisting of lung images affected by emphysema and other conditions, and the results show that it significantly enhances classification accuracy and robustness by a substantial margin compared to baseline methods.

This study aims to find sufficient and necessary conditions for a certain class of weighted $L_p$ interpolation projectors to have their norm strictly less than one, and it also presents examples of weights that result in an arbitrary bound for the norm of such projectors when considering the space $L_p$, where $1\leq p<\infty$, on the interval $(-1,1)$.

For an irreducible graph $G$ and associated random walk $X$, we'll introduce a specific transition probability matrix $M$ derived from $X$. We'll then establish a characteristic polynomial $\Phi_M$ for matrix $M$ in terms of a self-intersection characteristic polynomial $\Phi_X$ related to graph $G$. This study extends previous findings, particularly those of Bacher and Saloff-Coste for simple random walks on $G$, to general associated walks and their corresponding transition probability matrices.

Discrete time systems, which are commonly modeled using infinite sequences of states, are often analyzed by incorporating equations that describe how these systems evolve. However, it has been demonstrated that some models, specifically those with countably infinite states, are incompatible with a consistent inclusion of time-based definitions in their framework. This paper investigates continuous time systems, which are typically modeled as functions from time to state, and it explores the implications of adding time-based definitions to the HOL framework for the purpose of verifying these systems using theorem provers. It also delves into how incorporating time-based definitions affects the properties of logical equivalence and encompasses the results of previous studies.

To develop efficient subgrid-scale models for simulations, researchers incorporate details from improved, data-driven models. A new framework combines enhanced information from direct simulations with coarse-scale models. In our study, enhanced models were derived from direct simulations of wall turbulence. When applied to grid data between walls, models accurately predict fluctuations in grid cells. Combining these models with existing coarse-scale models yields improved estimates of increased grid cell fluctuations. However, direct simulations reveal significant turbulence issues that challenge existing theories. Combining the improved models with existing theories for increased grid cell fluctuations significantly improves their accuracy. A comparison with high-resolution simulations shows the improved models have lower errors than existing industry standards for simulating turbulence.

We demonstrate the connection between a particular N=1 supersymmetric Born-Infeld Skyrme model and a complex matrix problem, which we use to study soliton solutions in four-dimensional theoretical frameworks. Through further analysis, we find a correspondence between the fermionic properties of these solitons and the solutions to a particular radial Dirac equation in a potential defined by a parameter. We utilize a particular approximation to this radial equation to derive the mass properties of the fermions, revealing interesting relationships with properties of bosonic solitons in the N=1 model and a simpler, non-Abelian Skyrme model.

For Weyl semimetals exhibiting Ruchi time-reversal symmetry breaking, there is a necessity to consider the interplay between magnetic flux and the Fermi surfaces. The presence of a magnetic field disrupts the continuity of the Fermi surface, resulting in the emergence of "Bullseye" structures characteristic of Landau levels. The "Bullseye" structures are accompanied by an anomalous Hall effect, driven by the unique topological properties of the material. Theoretical research into the electronic structure of "Bullseye" topological crystals is ongoing. The authors of this study have identified a specific Weyl crystal that can be analyzed in the Hofstadter regime, demonstrating a unique case where R and P symmetries are preserved. The numerical simulation of the electronic structure of this material has yielded "Bullseye" structures, along with pairs of Weyl nodes, resulting in a novel topological arrangement. Theoretical predictions suggest that the intensity of the Weyl nodes and their spatial arrangement exhibit periodicity, governed by the magnetic flux density and interaction strength parameters. Theoretical models show that the magnetic field's effect on the material is more significant at lower lattice sizes and higher mass anisotropy values. Theoretical simulations demonstrate that the magnetic field's effect on the material is more significant at lower lattice sizes and higher interaction strength parameters.

Recent advancements in nanotechnology have led to a surge in miniaturization,
utilizing two-dimensional metal and dielectric structures for controlling light.
Despite their light absorption issues, metallic nanoantennas offer significant
advantages in terms of concentration and transfer of electromagnetic energy.
This hybrid research combines the strengths of both plasmonic and dielectric
nanotechnology to develop an innovative hybrid nanoantenna for highly efficient,
luminous photon sources. By combining these components, we can enhance the
radiation patterns of the source, leading to increased photon emission rates,
potentially up to 50 times greater than traditional methods, through optimal
tuning of the metal and dielectric materials' properties.

The screening phenomenon, particularly notable in granular matter, is a crucial feature of its behavior. An advanced numerical model has been developed to accurately simulate the static properties of a granular assembly at a microscopic level, eliminating the need for an empirical friction coefficient. This sophisticated algorithm, known as the Anomalous Screening model (ASM), has been tested through experiments involving compacted and force-chain imaging of monodisperse granular clusters. Comparison of results from experiments and numerical simulations shows impressive correlation, especially regarding friction coefficients and force distribution patterns. These findings provide strong evidence for ASM's efficacy and its potential applications in accurately predicting the friction behavior of complex granular systems.

The properties properties are properties are computed by the Density Functional Theory, employing the PBESol functional within a plane wave pseudopotential framework. Hexagonal arrangements of Mn atoms on the silicene surface were examined, and a significant lattice mismatch was observed, yet the substrate allows for the preservation of the moiré pattern. The interaction between Mn and the substrate yields a significant energy gain, primarily due to the interaction between Mn and Si atoms. Hexagonal arrangements of Mn atoms exhibit the greatest stability, displaying a magnetic saturation of approximately 4.95 µB per moment. The interaction between Mn and the substrate significantly alters the electronic properties of the material. The system's behavior is characterized by a semiconductor behavior with a significant indirect bandgap of approximately 0.42 eV. The spin-polarized characteristics of the material are preserved, yet the carrier type and bandgap size are heavily influenced by the interaction with the substrate. A supernova remnant known as Sgr A East, located at the center of our galaxy, has a rich 11,000-year history. The origin of this phenomenon remains a source of interest, particularly in understanding the precise location of the supernova event that led to Sgr A East's formation. The theory suggesting that Sgr A East was created by a supernova occurring within our galaxy's core has been particularly appealing due to its simplicity. However, alternative theories propose that it might have been caused by a supernova occurring nearby before the star was incorporated into the galactic core. To explore these possibilities, the 3D simulation code SIMBA was used to model possible scenarios in which a supernora occurred in the immediate vicinity of the galactic core under the influence of strong tidal forces. The goal of the investigation was to determine the precise location of the supernova event that could potentially explain Sgr A East's formation by replicating its gas shell and overall dimensions. The results revealed that the most likely explanation lies in a supernora occurring within the galactic core, under the influence of strong tidal forces. Specifically, simulations indicate that a supernova occurring at a distance of approximately 1.5 parsecs from the galactic core, combined with a core mass of approximately 4 million solar masses, best replicate the observed gas shell of Sgr A East. Text classification systems face the issue of class imbalance when dealing with multi-class labels, which can lead to suboptimal performance and inaccurate predictions for underrepresented categories. To address this challenge, researchers often apply data augmentation techniques to increase the number of samples for minority classes. In this research, we examine the effectiveness of four different data augmentation techniques on a news categorization dataset and investigate their impact on the performance of machine learning models for text classification.

This study investigates the correlation between COVID-19 coverage in U.S. local news and a variety of factors, including pandemic indicators, political dynamics, and socio-economic conditions. With data on over 900 U.S. local news programs spanning more than a year, this research reveals that COVID-19 coverage is influenced by a complex interplay of cases, deaths, and other variables. Notably, demographic and socio-economic characteristics play a crucial role in shaping the content of news reports. The findings also show that the disparity in COVID-19 coverage between rural and urban areas correlates with demographic and socio-economic differences.

The preservation of angular momentum remains crucial in particle simulations, particularly for modeling complex interactions among celestial bodies. Our research focuses on integrating the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) with the constraint of angular momentum conservation within a symplectic framework. Complex multipole expansions are proposed, allowing for more accurate models of non-rigid bodies, while applying a constraint correction based on a modified impulse method. Experimental validation of our approach is demonstrated for advanced multipole expansions.

This paper presents the outcomes of the initial experiment, utilizing a polarized proton target, undertaken at the HIFREQ spectrometer within the HRS experimental setup, with the reaction $e^-\vec{p} \to e^-\vec{p}$ as its focus. The polarized, hydrogen gas target, developed by IHEP, was employed to measure the transfer of proton polarization in the elastic reaction $e^-\vec{p} \to e^-\vec{p}$ through measurements of the double differential cross section and the polarization transfer coefficient $E/G$. The cross-sectional measurements matched the predictions of the Rosenbluth formula, while the experimental findings for the polarization transfer coefficient were compared with the predictions of a relativistic potential model by Dickel and Strakovsky.

This study investigates the potential of adopting a recently introduced system, 
the Policy Learning with Order-Independent Expert Set (POLINE), which allows 
agents to efficiently learn from a collection of ordered experts. We identify 
two main drawbacks of the POLINE framework in terms of implementation: first, 
agents often struggle to effectively learn from environments they cannot directly 
experience due to high expert diversity and restricted access to experiences from 
unutilized experts; second, given environment complexity, learning rates required 
on experienced experts are typically low, leading to prolonged training times. 
To address these issues, we propose two novel modifications to the POLINE 
framework: first, we introduce a virtual experience generation approach that 
enables agents to efficiently learn from experiences from unused experts; 
second, we suggest adjusting expert learning rates in line with experience 
distribution to improve efficiency. 
Experimental results show that these modifications yield notable improvements 
in terms of training efficiency and overall performance when compared to the 
original POLINE framework.

Researchers have been exploring the production of a pair of Higgs bosons linked with a vector boson using the ATLAS detector and 13 TeV proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider.  They've analyzed a combined dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected between 2015 and 2016 in various channels, primarily focusing on the $WZ$ and $ZZ$ boson pairs.  The Higgs bosons' decays into a pair of photons or into $b$-quarks' pairs were the chosen channels, but decays involving final state leptons and jets were also considered.  The findings show no evidence of these $HH$ processes, which were constrained to cross-sections ranging from 1.3 to 8.4 times the Higgs bosons' SM-predicted rates in comparison to a similar ratio of $pp$ → $VH$ production of $VH$ where the Higgs decays into $b$-quarks.  This study also derived limits on certain Beyond the Standard Model phenomena, which were found to affect the Higgs-V boson coupling strength, particularly in relation to the gluon-Higgs-V boson triangle loop phenomenon.  These limits were found to correspond to ratios of $\left|c_g/\delta_g\right|$ ranging from 0.44 to 0.93.

We introduce the concept of a spin laser that generates spin 3/2 sodium digital matter through the use of a traveling-wave modulated optical potential, which induces coherent emissions of up to ten traveling-wave stimulated emission peaks per atom. This corresponds to a coherent emission of ten orbital angular momentum states, which is achieved by a digital alteration of the environment that couples to a highly-driven internal degree of freedom, thereby producing multiple quantum systems with discrete energy levels that undergo simultaneous, digital-stimulated emission of equidistant frequencies. The theoretical foundation of this idea relies on precise control of atomic degrees of freedom and may lead to significant advancements in quantum information processing and metrology with aid of discrete-time coherent light and matter sources.

For the given family of K3 surfaces defined by $X_t = \{z \in \mathbb{C}^4: z \cdot z = t\}$, we calculate the Picard values, specifically the upper and lower limits $v^+(t)$ and $v^-(t)$, which represent the maximum and minimum degrees of map from $X_t$ to any related elliptic Kummer surface. We find lower and upper bounds, $4|t|^{-1/2}$ and $|t|^{-1}$, and prove these values grow to infinity as $t$ approaches 0 within the Siegel disk radius $e^{-\pi}$ and also show this growth holds for the larger radius $2e^{-\pi}$.

A neutralino is considered a viable dark matter candidate, where its lifetime is the primary factor influencing both direct detection and gamma ray observation methods. The most significant gammaray signal resulting from neutralino decay is the difference between the masses of the dark matter and lightest supersymmetric particle. Assuming a 100 GeV mass for the neutralino and a lifetime exceeding $10^{21}$ seconds, the predicted gammaray background from the decay of extragalactic gamma ray sources is analyzed, utilizing 130 terrestrial and 7 space-borne experiments' data, which collectively constrain the decay process. The current study finds that the predicted gammaray background is most limited for neutralino masses approximately 60-70 GeV, particularly in the 2-30 MeV energy range, which is notably lower than the neutralino mass used in previous studies. The analysis further explores the implications of varying supersymmetry parameters, particularly focusing on the mu term and trilinear soft parameter's ratio, which may allow neutralino decay to be the dominant dark matter annihilation mechanism for specific mass ranges, with masses approximately 100-120 GeV, which is particularly relevant to the LSP LHC production zone, utilizing a b-bino LSP mass scenario.

We have developed a novel, log n-approximation algorithm for estimating the genus of a given undirected simple graph in GGen, an advanced version of the Shortest Non-Hyperplanar Subgraph problem. GGen offers an enhanced approximation factor compared to the current best algorithm, providing log n / e2 approximation. Moreover, we've demonstrated that achieving even a constant approximation factor in log n is an NP-hard problem, showing that our algorithm represents perhaps the best possible result. To reach this outcome, we've created a new algorithm that identifies a diverse set of non-Planar subgraphs in linear time, drawing on results from the Densest Subgraph and Dirac's Theorem.

A versatile algorithm is developed for executing convex optimization tasks across distributed systems, leveraging random communication connections. Employing a stochastic algorithm without requiring explicit neighbor information, it utilizes randomly selected communication partners to exchange solely local gradient/weight data. By leveraging a stochastic Newton update approach, both the communication and computational complexities achieve near-optimal performance without random neighbor sampling.

Our approach to training a neural network involves utilizing word embeddings derived from pre-trained models, specifically the multilingual version of word2vec, as well as a neural word embedding model that incorporates dropout as a means of regularization.

Next-generation dark matter experiments utilizing time projection chambers with
gaseous detection mediums have the potential to identify nuclear recoils triggered
by cosmic rays or neutrinos. This capability enables the exclusion of backgrounds
from solar neutrinos that typically interfere with the search for dark matter.
This research investigates the characteristics of the most effective
observables for identifying full- and multi-peak recoils in high-resolution
time projection chambers with large volumes. A detailed study of the
reconstruction of the direction of the recoil, in conjunction with the energy of
the particle's interaction and the volume of the gas above the electron track, is
presented as the core components of this research. Additionally, the study
evaluates the potential of combining these individual features into a single,
comprehensive indicator through a multi-dimensional clustering approach.
Results from this research are supplemented by simulation studies of detailed
instrumentation and a comprehensive overview of the relevant underlying
phenomena, including electron diffusion, signal loss due to noise and other
factors. PANCY, a conceptual experiment for the direct observation of dark
matter through nuclear recoils, is used to illustrate the potential of this
research. PANCY is envisioned as a large-scale, pressurized detector filled with
a mixture of isobutane and neon, with precise 3D reconstruction capabilities to
